questions.stem: A student examines a cadaver's liver, femur, and heart with the naked eye, noting their shapes and how they sit relative to one another. Which field is this?
questions.why: Gross anatomy is the study of large body structures — bones, heart, liver — that can be seen without magnification. Microscopic anatomy requires magnification, and physiology addresses function rather than structure.

options.why: That is the study of function, not structure.
That is the microscopic study of tissues.
That requires a microscope, not the naked eye.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines physiology?
questions.why: Physiology is the study of function — how the body and its parts work as a single unit. Structure and shape belong to anatomy.

options.t: How disease alters the body's structures
options.why: That is pathology, the study of disease.

options.t: How body parts are named and classified
options.why: That is anatomical terminology, not physiology.

options.t: How the body and its parts function together
How the body and its parts are structured
options.why: That is anatomy, the study of structure.

questions.stem: Anatomy is the study of structure. Beyond the shape of the body and its parts, what else does that definition include?
questions.why: The definition covers the shape of the body and its parts AND the relationships between those structures. Relationship is part of anatomy, not an add-on.

options.why: Energy production is a physiological process.

options.t: How structures relate to one another

options.why: Aging changes are one topic within anatomy, not its definition.
Drug response belongs to pharmacology.

questions.stem: Anatomical structure determines physiological function. How many lobes does each lung have?
questions.why: Left lung has 2 lobes, right lung has 3 — the left is smaller to accommodate the heart. The anatomy (5 lobes total) enables the physiology (gas exchange).

options.why: The left lung has fewer lobes than the right.
Neither lung has three lobes on the left.
The lobe counts are reversed here.

questions.stem: Applying the same structure-determines-function principle to the heart: how many chambers does it have, and what is its physiological role?
questions.why: Anatomy: 4 chambers. Physiology: pumps blood. Oxygenation happens in the lungs, not the heart.

options.why: Oxygenation happens in the lungs, not the heart.
The human heart has four chambers, not three.
Two chambers cannot separate oxygenated from deoxygenated blood.

questions.stem: How many organ systems make up the human body?
questions.why: There are 12 systems: integumentary, skeletal, muscular, nervous, endocrine, cardiovascular, respiratory, immune, lymphatic, digestive, urinary, and reproductive.

options.why: That is close but still short of the total.
That overstates the number of systems.
That undercounts the organ systems.

questions.stem: Both the nervous and endocrine systems act as control centers of the body. What distinguishes the two?
questions.why: Both are control centers, but the route differs: the nervous system uses rapid electrical impulses, while the endocrine system sends hormones through the blood. That difference is why endocrine responses are slower and longer-lasting.

options.t: Nervous controls through electrical impulses; endocrine controls through the blood
Nervous is involuntary only; endocrine is voluntary only
options.why: The nervous system includes voluntary control too.

options.t: Nervous controls through the blood; endocrine controls through electrical impulses
options.why: The blood is the endocrine route, not the nervous one.

options.t: Nervous acts on organs; endocrine acts only on muscle
options.why: Both systems act on organs and tissues.

questions.stem: Which system is responsible for returning fluid that has leaked out of the circulatory system back to the blood vessels?
questions.why: The lymphatic system maintains body fluid levels, removes cellular waste, and returns leaked fluid to the blood vessels. The immune system is separate — it is the white-blood-cell response to infection.

options.why: That defends against pathogens.
That removes nitrogen waste rather than returning fluid.
That circulates blood rather than draining tissue fluid.

questions.stem: The urinary system removes nitrogen-containing wastes. Which two are they?
questions.why: Urea and uric acid are the nitrogen-containing wastes; they can break down proteins and nucleic acids, so they have to be flushed out.

options.why: Bilirubin comes from red cell breakdown, not the kidney.
Creatinine belongs in the list instead of one of these.
Ammonia is the third product named alongside these.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly lists the structures air passes through in the respiratory system?
questions.why: Air travels nasal passage, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, then lungs. The larynx sits below the pharynx and above the trachea — a distinction that matters when you're managing an airway.

options.t: Nasal passage → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → lungs
Nasal passage → pharynx → trachea → larynx → bronchi → lungs
options.why: The larynx is missing from this sequence.

options.t: Pharynx → nasal passage → trachea → larynx → lungs → bronchi
options.why: Air enters the nose before reaching the pharynx.

options.t: Nasal passage → larynx → pharynx → trachea → bronchi → lungs
options.why: The larynx sits below the pharynx, not above it.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of the muscular system?
questions.why: The muscular system allows manipulation, maintains posture, produces facial expressions, and generates heat. Blood cell production is a skeletal system function (marrow).

options.why: Movement is the primary muscular function.
Posture is maintained by sustained muscle tone.
Muscle activity is a major heat source.

questions.stem: Which structures make up the skeletal system?
questions.why: Bones, cartilage, ligaments, and joints — important for structure and protection. Tendons attach muscle to bone and are grouped with the muscular system here.

options.why: None of these are the skeletal framework itself.
Vessels and skin are not skeletal structures.
Tendons and nerves belong to other systems.

questions.stem: The integumentary system is the external covering of the body. Which set of functions does it perform?
questions.why: Skin regulates temperature, hydrates, and prevents injuries. It's the body's external covering and first barrier.

options.t: Temperature regulation, sensation, and blood cell production
options.why: These are integumentary functions but the question asks what it covers.

options.t: Injury prevention, digestion, and waste removal
options.why: Digestion is not an integumentary function.

options.t: Temperature regulation, hydration, and injury prevention

options.why: Hormone secretion is an endocrine role.

questions.stem: Which of these is listed as part of the lymphatic system?
questions.why: The lymphatic system includes lymph, lymphatic vessels, lymph nodes, lymphatic tissues, the spleen, and the tonsils.

options.why: The thyroid is endocrine, not lymphatic.
Both are endocrine organs.
Both are digestive accessory organs.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines homeostasis?
questions.why: Homeostasis is the ability to maintain a stable internal environment despite external change. It is the shared goal of all 12 organ systems.

options.t: Returning conditions to their newborn state
options.why: Conditions are not returned to any earlier state.

options.t: Keeping internal conditions stable amid change

options.why: Homeostasis allows fluctuation within a range.

options.t: Matching internal conditions to the environment
options.why: The body defends its own set point rather than matching outside.

questions.stem: The root 'stasis' means standing still, which makes the term homeostasis misleading. Why?
questions.why: The name suggests something unchanging, but homeostasis is active and dynamic: the body constantly makes changes to hold balance. Those changes don't have to be large.

options.t: No change occurs once balance is reached
options.why: Constant adjustment continues even at balance.

options.t: Change occurs only during illness or stress
options.why: Adjustment happens continuously in health too.

options.t: The set point drifts, so balance is only ever approximate
options.why: Set points do move with age and conditioning, but the body still holds each one actively — that drift is not what makes the word misleading.

options.t: Change constantly occurs to hold balance

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a receptor?
questions.why: A receptor can be an organ, tissue, cell, or molecule that responds to a stimulus — light, heat, a neurotransmitter, a hormone, an antigen, and so on. It is not limited to nerve endings or to one stimulus type.

options.t: A structure that responds to a stimulus
A structure that carries out the correction
options.why: That describes the effector.

options.t: A structure that stores the normal set point
options.why: Storing the set point is a control center role.

options.t: A structure that issues corrective orders
options.why: That describes the control center.

questions.stem: An afferent pathway carries information in which direction?
questions.why: Afferent = arriving at the CNS. Efferent = exiting the CNS toward the body. If you mix these up, the whole reflex loop reverses.

options.t: From the endocrine glands to the blood
options.why: Hormones travel in blood, not afferent pathways.
Peripheral nerves relay to the CNS, not to each other.

options.t: Away from the CNS to the body
options.why: That is the efferent direction.

questions.stem: After the CNS analyzes incoming information and determines a response, that response travels along which pathway?
questions.why: Efferent pathways carry the response (change, impulse, stimulus) from the CNS out to the body.

options.why: A reflex is a response pattern, not a pathway name.
Afferent carries information toward the CNS.
The receptor detects the change.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the homeostatic feedback loop?
questions.why: A receptor detects the stimulus and sends it via the afferent pathway to the CNS; the CNS determines the appropriate response and sends it via the efferent pathway; feedback then returns to the CNS to check whether further change is needed.

options.t: Receptor → afferent pathway → CNS analysis → efferent pathway → feedback
Receptor → efferent pathway → CNS analysis → afferent pathway → feedback
options.why: The efferent pathway comes after CNS analysis.

options.t: Afferent pathway → receptor → efferent pathway → CNS analysis → feedback
options.why: The receptor precedes the afferent pathway.

options.t: CNS analysis → receptor → afferent pathway → feedback → efferent pathway
options.why: The receptor must act before the CNS can analyze.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the feedback step in the homeostatic loop?
questions.why: Feedback is sent back to the CNS so it can determine whether the response worked or whether more adjustment is required. That loop is what keeps the system self-correcting.

options.t: To detect the original change in conditions
options.why: That is the receptor's job.

options.t: To set the normal range the body defends
options.why: The set point is established, not reported by feedback.

options.t: To tell the CNS whether more change is needed
To carry the correction out to the organs
options.why: That is the efferent pathway's job.

questions.stem: How many basic levels of organization does the body have, and in what order do they progress?
questions.why: Six levels, progressing simplest to most complex: chemical → cellular → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.

options.t: Eight, from atomic up to population
options.why: That overstates the number of levels.

options.t: Six, from organism down to chemical
options.why: The sequence runs simplest to most complex.

options.t: Four, from cellular up to organism
options.why: That skips the chemical and tissue levels.

options.t: Six, from chemical up to organism

questions.stem: Which level of organization sits directly between tissue and organ system?
questions.why: An organ is a collection of tissues forming a functional unit; a group of organs working together forms an organ system.

options.why: Chemical is the simplest level of all.
Organism is the most complex level.
Cellular sits below tissue, not above it.

questions.stem: The word 'organism' derives from organize + -ism. What principle does that reflect?
questions.why: The word itself signals that organization is what allows the body to function as a whole — each level builds on the one below it.

options.t: Organs are the basic unit of all life
options.why: The cell, not the organ, is the basic living unit.

options.t: Organisms are defined by their cell count
options.why: Cell count does not define an organism.

options.t: Living things must reproduce to qualify
options.why: Reproduction is one characteristic of life, not the principle here.

options.t: Organization underpins how the body works

questions.stem: Among the characteristics shared by all living things, how is respiration defined?
questions.why: Respiration here is the cellular definition: using food sources in combination with oxygen to release energy. Converting food into simpler compounds is digestion; moving air is ventilation.

options.t: Using food and oxygen to release energy

options.why: That describes absorption.

options.t: Removing waste products from the body
options.why: That describes excretion.

options.t: Producing offspring of the same kind
options.why: That describes reproduction.

questions.stem: Which characteristic of life is defined as the ability to respond to internal and external stimuli?
questions.why: Responsiveness is reacting to stimuli. Movement is changing location or position, or moving internal structures.

options.why: That is converting absorbed materials into body substance.
That is specialization of cells into distinct types.
That is producing new individuals.

questions.stem: Absorption, as a characteristic of life, refers to what?
questions.why: Absorption is the movement of material through membranes. Moving substances via body fluids is circulation, removing waste is excretion, and increasing in size is growth.

options.why: That is digestion.
That is secretion into the blood.

options.t: Moving materials along the digestive tract
options.why: That is movement through the tract, not absorption.

questions.stem: Match each organ system to its description.
questions.why: The cardiovascular and lymphatic systems both move fluid, and the nervous and endocrine systems are both control centers — the difference is always the mechanism, not the goal.
pairs: Moves oxygen and nutrients to all the body's tissues
Breaks down what you eat to the chemical level for the body to use
White blood cells fighting off infection, toxins, and bacteria
Removes nitrogen-containing waste and flushes it out
Control center working through electrical impulses
Control center working through the blood

questions.stem: Match each level of organization to its definition.
questions.why: Each level is built from the one before it. Knowing the order matters more than the exact wording — chemical is simplest, organism is most complex.
pairs: Material of which animals or plants are made
A collection of tissues forming a functional unit
A group of organs working together for one or more functions
